questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A performance and what survives of it
questions.learningObjective: Identify what documentation preserves of a performance
questions.stem: A clerk's note records a performance that was documented only by photographs, and asks what the record preserves.

options.text: The record preserves appearances at chosen instants, so duration and sequence survive only as inference
The record preserves the performance in full, since a complete series of photographs reproduces every moment
options.misconception: believes a photo series carries the whole event

options.text: The record preserves only what the camera could not see, since visible material is captured by memory
options.misconception: reverses what a document retains and what it misses

options.text: The record preserves the legal conditions of the event, so a gallery may rely on it as evidence
options.misconception: treats a photographic record as a legal instrument

questions.explanation: Photographs fix appearances at selected instants, so they carry evidence of appearance, not of duration or sequence. A complete series, an inverted account and a legal reading each overreach.
questions.hint: Ask what a single frame can and cannot show about time.

questions.explanation: The lines left unperformed are 30 minus 22, which is 8. Reading the figure of 22 as the number of lines carried out plus the remainder would give 14 and double-count the completed lines.
questions.hint: Take the completed lines away from the total.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the camera took over from painting
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a photograph differs in evidentiary status from a painting
questions.stem: A memorandum explains how a photograph of a performance differs in kind from a painting of the same subject.

answer.exemplar: A painting of a performance is a report of what the painter saw, and it is answerable to the painter's judgement about what was worth showing, so it can be invented, arranged or improved upon. A photograph of the same event is tied to the light that actually reached the lens during an exposure, and it cannot be adjusted without altering what it claims to record. That difference in how the two are answerable is what the camera took over from painting, and it is why a photographed event can be treated as evidence of appearance while a painted one is treated as evidence of a viewpoint.

questions.explanation: A painting answers to the painter's judgement and can be arranged, while a photograph is bound to the light that reached the lens. That is the shift in what a picture can be evidence of.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two can be altered and still remain itself.

options.text: Few visitors stayed, so the installation's dependence on the room is clearly a weakness in the design
options.misconception: inverts the majority into a failure

options.text: Most visitors stayed, so the installation could be moved into a larger hall without any change to its effect
options.misconception: concludes mobility from attendance figures

questions.explanation: A large majority remaining more than five minutes supports the idea that the work and its room hold attention together. A general ranking, an inverted reading and portability each overreach.
questions.hint: Read the proportion before concluding about the room.

questions.topic: A poster read from a distance
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a poster must sacrifice to be legible at distance

stimulus.body: A district archive holds a poster whose central element is a single face rendered at 40 centimetres high, printed in a dark ink on a pale ground, with a line of condensed capitals running beneath it. The remaining surface carries fine shading and small print that is only legible from within a metre of the sheet. A note in the file records that the poster was intended for display across a busy road.

questions.stem: A clerk summarises a poster in a district archive and asks what it says when read from a distance.

options.text: The face and the single line carry the message, while the fine shading and small print are expendable
The face and the single line carry the message, while the fine shading and small print are worth most
options.misconception: judges a poster by what a close reader can extract

options.text: The fine shading and small print carry the message, since detail survives best at a distance in poor light
options.misconception: claims detail survives distance better than mass does

options.text: The face and the single line carry the message, while the shading and small print show two production stages
options.misconception: reads a difference in detail as two production stages

questions.explanation: At road distance only mass, contrast and short lines survive, so the face and capitals do the work. A close-read valuation, detail over mass and a two-stage story each misjudge what distance allows.
questions.hint: Ask which elements can still be read at thirty metres.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A framed list of instructions
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a list of instructions behaves differently from a list of statements
questions.stem: A clerk asks why a framed list of instructions behaves differently from a framed list of statements about the same subject.

answer.exemplar: A list of statements is complete on the wall. It can be read, disagreed with, quoted and left, because nothing in it asks the reader to do anything, and the sheet retains its meaning whatever the reader does next. A list of instructions is not complete there at all: it is a set of directions to a reader who will act, so the work exists only when the acts are performed, and a reader who leaves without acting has read a programme rather than a work. The frame cannot change this, since what the sheet carries is an instruction, and the difference lies in whether the reader's body is required.

questions.explanation: A statement is finished when read, while an instruction is only carried out by acting, so the latter needs the reader's body. The frame cannot alter that difference between reading and performing.
questions.hint: Ask whether the sheet is complete once it has been read.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A performance and what survives of it
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate whether a record of a performance is the performance
questions.stem: A file note considers whether a photograph of a performance is the performance itself.

answer.exemplar: It is not, and the reason is not that the photograph is a poor substitute but that it is a different kind of object with a different relation to what happened. A performance exists only while it is being performed, in a specific place and time, and it is complete in itself at the moment of its completion. A photograph of one is a subsequent object that can be moved, sold, framed and re-read, and it fixes a set of instants rather than a duration. It may be the only surviving carrier of the event, and it may be the strongest claim anyone has to make about it, but it stands beside the performance as its record rather than in its place.

questions.explanation: A performance exists only in its own occurrence, while a photograph is a later, movable object fixing instants rather than a duration. It is the record of the event, not a substitute for it.
questions.hint: Ask what each of the two is, and when it exists.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A memorial cut into the ground
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a memorial's site contributes that a photograph of it cannot
questions.stem: A second case memo asks what the site of a memorial contributes that a photograph of the same site does not.

answer.exemplar: The site carries the visitor's body, the walk and the weather, and the cut names only register properly when a person stands at the scale of the stone and reads along a line that is set into the ground. A photograph flattens all of that into a picture: it fixes one viewpoint, crops the ground out of the frame, and turns a surface that can be walked across into an image that can only be looked at. The site is therefore part of the memorial's argument rather than its setting, and the record of it, useful as it is, is a different kind of object from the thing it records.

questions.explanation: The site involves the body, the walk and the scale, none of which a photograph can hold, so the cut is part of the argument, not a setting. The record and the memorial are different kinds of object.
questions.hint: Ask what the body does at the site that a camera cannot.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the camera took over from painting
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the camera changed the evidence an exhibition could hold
questions.stem: A memorandum explains how the camera changed the kind of evidence an exhibition is able to hold.

answer.exemplar: Before the camera, an exhibition of pictures could offer views and arguments, and the strongest claim any of them made was that a person had stood before a subject and chosen to show it this way. Once the camera existed, an exhibition could also hold a claim about how something actually appeared at a moment, and that claim came with the standing of a trace rather than a report. The change did not abolish the older kind of picture but it reorganised the room, because a photograph competed for the wall by promising something painting could not promise, and viewers began to read all pictures, painted ones included, against that promise of record.

questions.explanation: The camera gave exhibitions a second claim, a trace of actual appearance, which reorganised how all pictures were read. The older view-based picture did not vanish but lost its monopoly.
questions.hint: Ask what new promise the camera brought to the wall.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the camera took over from painting
questions.learningObjective: Explain what the camera borrowed from painting and what it refused
questions.stem: A file note considers what the camera borrowed from painting and what it refused to take from it.

answer.exemplar: The camera borrowed the whole apparatus of the single framed picture, the rectangle on the wall, the option to be hung at the eye's height and the privilege of being looked at one at a time, and it took that so completely that the painted picture is now read as an early form of the same thing. What it refused was the painter's privilege of intervention. A painted surface may be constructed in a studio, adjusted, invented and improved, and it remains a report of a person looking. The camera kept the frame and gave up the hand, and that exchange is why a photograph could take painting's place on the wall without also taking painting's claim to be made by a person.

questions.explanation: The camera inherited the framed, single, eye-level picture and refused the painter's privilege of invention and adjustment. That exchange let it take painting's place without taking its authorship.
questions.hint: Ask what the camera kept from the older picture and gave up.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A performance and what survives of it
questions.learningObjective: Explain what survives of a performance once the event has ended
questions.stem: A memorandum asks what survives of a performance once the event itself is over.

answer.exemplar: What survives falls into three quite different kinds, and keeping them apart matters. The first is the record: photographs, programmes, scores, costumes and accounts, each of which carries some part of the work and none of which is the work. The second is the reputation, which is a claim made later by others and can be accurate, flattering or invented. The third is the possibility of repetition, which depends on the work having been written or instructed down in a form that allows it to be performed again, and this is the only kind of survival that lets the work occur anew rather than being discussed. A performance without any of these is gone, though it may still be remembered as a name.

questions.explanation: Records, later reputation and the possibility of repetition are three survivals, and only the last allows the work to happen again. Without any of them the event is over, even if its name persists.
questions.hint: Ask which of the survivals could make the work happen again.

questions.topic: An installation that depends on its room
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an installation's meaning changes when it is relocated
questions.stem: A case memo asks how an installation's meaning changes when it is moved to another room.

answer.exemplar: The meaning does not travel with the objects, because much of what an installation says is said by the room in which it stands. Height, light, acoustics and the direction of approach are all parts of the work's argument, and a different room supplies different ones, so the moved installation becomes a different work that happens to use the same pieces. This is why such works are often described as inseparable from their site, and it is also why the decision to move one is an interpretive act rather than a logistical one, requiring someone to decide what the work was really about and whether that reading can survive the move.

questions.explanation: Height, light, acoustics and approach are part of the argument, so a move produces a different work from the same pieces. Relocation is therefore an interpretive decision, not a logistics problem.
questions.hint: Ask what the new room supplies that the old one did not.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What indexicality does and does not license
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a photograph is not a machine-made painting
questions.stem: A memorandum explains why a photograph is not simply a painting that happens to be made by a machine.

answer.exemplar: The difference is not mechanical but contractual. A painting is an arrangement of marks by a person, and every compositional decision is answerable to that person's intention, so the finished surface can be moved, retouched or invented without ceasing to be a painting of its subject. A photograph is a set of consequences: the shutter opened, light fell, and the plate or film recorded what reached it, and the maker's decisions are confined to framing, focus, exposure and the choice of moment. The machine does not paint because it cannot intend the arrangement, and the photograph therefore stakes its claim not on what anyone decided but on what the light did, which is why it can serve as evidence where a painting can only serve as testimony.

questions.explanation: A painting answers to intention and can be invented; a photograph answers to physical consequences the maker does not control. That is why a photograph testifies while a painting only speaks.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two can be altered and still remain itself.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A memorial cut into the ground
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an inscription turns individuals into a public record
questions.stem: A memorandum asks how a memorial's cut names convert individual people into a public record.

answer.exemplar: The cut is a piece of writing in a public place, and that is what converts a life into an entry. Each name is reduced to the one thing the record can hold, set in a sequence governed by an arbitrary rule of order, and read by a stream of strangers who will never know the person named. In making the name legible to anyone who passes, the memorial confers a kind of permanence on the name while detaching it from everything else that was true of the person, which is precisely the exchange the practice involves. The visitor's own reading completes the work, and each reader becomes briefly the keeper of an entry that was never written for them.

questions.explanation: An inscription in a public place reduces a life to a name in a sequence and makes it legible to strangers, detaching the name from the person. Each passer-by briefly keeps the entry.
questions.hint: Ask what a name set into a public surface gains and loses.

questions.topic: A poster read from a distance
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a poster aimed at a passing vehicle must do differently
questions.stem: A poster intended to be read from a moving vehicle demands a different design from a close-read sheet, and a note asks why.

answer.exemplar: A viewer in a moving vehicle gets a fraction of a second in which the image must be taken in, so the sheet has to do its work at once and in a single glance. The message must be reducible to one element and a few words, the contrast has to be strong enough to survive the small fraction of the field of view it occupies, and the detail has to be abandoned rather than minimised, because a reader who is moving will never return to it. This is the opposite of the print made to be read, where the reward is on the second and third look, and the two kinds of sheet are not better and worse versions of one another but answers to entirely different conditions of looking.

questions.explanation: A moving reader has a fraction of a second, so the sheet must reduce to one element and strong contrast, abandoning detail. It answers to a different condition of looking than a print made to be read.
questions.hint: Ask how long a passing reader has and what can be taken in.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What indexicality does and does not license
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the claim that a photograph of a real place is a picture of that place
questions.stem: A note asks whether a photograph of a real place is thereby a picture of that place.

answer.exemplar: It is a picture of that place in one sense and not in another, and the difference is the whole of the matter. The image is causally connected to the place, and the light that made it came from the actual surfaces there, so it inherits a real trace of the site and is bound to it in a way an invented image is not. But a picture of a place is also a composition, a crop, a moment, a distance and a light, and every one of those is a decision that shaped what was recorded, so the frame in front of the viewer is a selection made from the place rather than the place itself. The trace is genuine and the picture is partial, and neither fact cancels the other.

questions.explanation: The image is genuinely connected to the place, but it is also a selection shaped by crop, moment and viewpoint. A real trace and a partial picture are both true at once.
questions.hint: Ask what the image received and what was chosen.

questions.topic: An installation that depends on its room
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a room contributes that a plan drawing of it cannot show
questions.stem: A memorandum asks what a room contributes to an installation that a measured plan of the same room cannot show.

answer.exemplar: A plan records extent and position, and every room has both, but a room is also an atmosphere and a sequence, and those are what the installation is usually working with. The height of the ceiling, the direction and hardness of the light, the reverberation of the floor, the smell of the material and the way a person feels their pace change on entering all belong to the room, and none of them can be read off a drawing of its outline. An installation that uses them is therefore working with something the plan omits, and a reconstruction built from the drawing alone would be dimensionally correct and practically inert, which is why the documents of such works tend to include photographs and measurements together.

questions.explanation: A plan gives extent and position, but height, light, acoustics and pace belong to the room as well. A reconstruction from the plan alone would be accurate and inert.
questions.hint: Ask what an outline drawing cannot tell you about the room.

questions.topic: A memorial cut into the ground
questions.learningObjective: Sequence what a memorial does with names into how its record falls short
questions.stem: Two steps are recorded for the memorial: what it does with the names it cuts, and how a photograph of it falls short.

options.text: It enters the names in a public order, and the photograph fixes one viewpoint and removes the walk
It enters the names in a public order, and the photograph cannot reproduce the lettering at all
options.misconception: overstates what a photograph is unable to show

options.text: It decorates the ground with names, and the photograph fixes one viewpoint and removes the walk
options.misconception: denies the commemorative work the names perform

options.text: It enters the names in a public order, and the photograph lacks the presence of the site entirely
options.misconception: denies the site a photograph can still show

questions.explanation: The memorial enters names into a public order, and a photograph of it loses the walk and the single viewpoint the site offers. Inability to show lettering and decoration each misread the limits.
questions.hint: Ask what the visitor does that a camera cannot follow.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the camera took over from painting
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the camera changed what a portrait could claim
questions.stem: A third case memo asks how the camera changed what a portrait could claim about its subject.

answer.exemplar: A painted portrait is a report of one person's encounter with another, and it is answerable to the sitter as much as to the painter, which is why such pictures were negotiated, revised and often disputed. The camera gave portraits a different footing, because the image is tied to light that actually fell on the sitter during an exposure, and it therefore supports a claim that the person was present before the lens in a way a painted likeness cannot. This did not make the camera's pictures more truthful about character, and painted portraits did not lose their power, but it did shift the question from who interpreted whom to what was in front of the apparatus, and the sitter's position within that arrangement became the business of the picture.

questions.explanation: The camera tied the portrait to a real encounter with the sitter, while the painted likeness remained a negotiated report. Character was not settled by this, but the terms of the exchange changed.
questions.hint: Ask what a painted likeness answers to, and photos do not.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What indexicality does and does not license
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the number of photographs recording subjects that still exist
questions.stem: An index of 100 photographs notes that 20 of them record subjects that no longer exist, the rest being of buildings, machines and people still present.
questions.explanation: The photographs of subjects still present are 100 minus 20, which is 80. Adding the two figures instead of subtracting would give 120, which is more photographs than the index lists.
questions.hint: Take the vanished subjects away from the total.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: An installation that depends on its room
questions.learningObjective: Explain what an installation's dependence on its room implies for ownership
questions.stem: A memorandum asks what an installation's dependence on its room implies for who owns the work and who may loan it.

answer.exemplar: The dependence unsettles the ordinary account of the work as a portable object with a single owner. If the room supplies height, light, acoustics and approach, then the thing owned is not only the set of materials but a relation between those materials and a particular space, and a loan that relocates them has altered the work rather than merely moved it. Two consequences follow. The owner of the site and the owner of the materials hold different and interdependent rights, and any loan has to be a joint decision rather than a transaction between two parties. And a work of this kind may be better described as belonging to its place than as held by an institution, which is a legal and ethical problem before it is an aesthetic one.

questions.explanation: If the room is part of the work, site and materials hold different rights, loans become joint decisions and relocation alters the work. Ownership is a legal and ethical problem, not a logistical one.
questions.hint: Ask who supplies the part of the work that cannot be packed.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A framed list of instructions
questions.learningObjective: Interpret reader reports about how a framed list was used
questions.stem: A visitor survey records 26 of 60 readers who said they read the framed list aloud, and 9 of those 26 said they carried out at least one line afterwards.

options.text: Reading aloud and carrying out are distinct steps, so reading is not the same as performing the work
Reading aloud and carrying out are distinct steps, so the survey shows the frame discourages acting
options.misconception: blames the frame for a failure the figures do not show

options.text: Reading aloud and carrying out are distinct steps, so 9 of 60 readers carried out a line of the list
options.misconception: uses 26 as the denominator instead of the 60 readers

options.text: Reading aloud and carrying out are distinct steps, so the framed list has no effect on how visitors behave
options.misconception: denies the frame any effect on visitor behaviour

questions.explanation: The figures separate a vocal reading from a performed act, and a third of those who read aloud then acted, so the two differ. A discouragement effect and a wrong denominator each misread it.
questions.hint: Keep the two stages separate and use the right base.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A poster read from a distance
questions.learningObjective: Analyse a poster whose message is carried by scale rather than detail

stimulus.body: A sheet in an archive carries a single word in letters 45 centimetres high, running the full width of the poster, with nothing else on the paper but a narrow band of colour along the lower edge. The word is set in a plain sans serif and the sheet is fixed to a wall at a junction where three footpaths meet. A record notes that the poster was replaced every fortnight, always with a single word in the same position.

questions.stem: A sheet in the archive carries its message by scale rather than detail, and a clerk asks what that means for how it works.

options.text: The single large word can be taken in at a glance, so the sheet is designed for the moment of approach
The single large word can be taken in at a glance, so the fortnightly replacement shows the message revised
options.misconception: reads a replacement schedule as revision of the message

options.text: The single large word can be taken in at a glance, so the narrow band of colour is the most important element
options.misconception: assigns the message to the colour band rather than the word

options.text: The single large word can be taken in at a glance, so the poster was designed to be read in detail at the wall
options.misconception: describes a glance-readable sheet as a close-reading design

questions.explanation: One large word is legible at a glance, so the sheet is built for the moment of approach rather than for sustained reading. Revision, a colour band and close reading each misread the described design.
questions.hint: Ask what a person on the move can manage to take in.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A performance and what survives of it
questions.learningObjective: Determine what documents of a performance can still establish
questions.stem: Two steps are settled for the file: what the performance involved, and what the surviving documents can still show.

options.text: It involved actions unfolding in a shared space, and the documents show appearance, order and instructions
It involved actions unfolding in a shared space, and the documents show each action's duration to the second
options.misconception: overstates what a document can fix about elapsed time

options.text: It involved a set of objects on display, and the documents show appearance, order and instructions
options.misconception: reduces the performance to a static display of objects

options.text: It involved actions unfolding in a shared space, and the documents show what every viewer felt
options.misconception: claims documents record the audience's emotional response

questions.explanation: Documents of a performance can establish appearance, order and the instructions issued, but not exact durations, object-based events or feeling. Each alternative overstates or misdescribes it.
questions.hint: Ask which records bear on time, order and on what was said.
